title: Fit a spin-on oil filter by hand to gasket contact, then to 18 N·m with a cap wrench on a ratchet, not loose or cranked
context: Automotive service technicians and mechanics (O*NET 49-3023.00, 825,800 US jobs in 2025 per BLS) change oil and filters as regular work. O*NET lists the task "Perform routine and scheduled maintenance services, such as oil changes, lubrications, and tune-ups", and a new filter is normally fitted at each oil change. The engine maker gives the filter a torque: Kawasaki's manual for the Teryx4, whose filter this is, gives 18 N·m, applied with a filter wrench after the gasket is oiled. Filter makers state the same fit as a turn: spin the filter on until its gasket contacts the base, then three quarters of a turn more. Left at contact it can work loose under vibration and leak; cranked well past a full turn it can crush its gasket, which can blow out under oil pressure. Here a new filter, started on a remote filter mount bolted to the bench, stops three quarters of a turn short of gasket contact; the wrench lies beside it.
setup: Positions are in cm from the midpoint between the two arm bases, with x forward, y to the robot's left and the table top at z 0. A die-cast aluminum remote oil filter mount (filter head) is bolted to the bench with four bolts: a block 7.5 cm deep (x), 9 cm wide (y) and 3.4 cm tall, with a round machined gasket land 7.2 cm across and 0.6 cm tall on top, so the gasket face is at z 4. Its threaded M20 x 1.5 nipple points straight up at x 30, y 30. Its two hose ports, on its left and right sides, are closed with gray plastic plugs, and a black witness line is painted on the front of the land and block. A new spin-on oil filter (Kawasaki 49065-0710), 250 g, is threaded onto the nipple: a black painted steel can 6.6 cm across and 7 cm tall with a plain flat top, grip flutes around its top edge, a white printed band, a black rubber gasket on its base, a printed index stripe down its side (white on the black, black across the band), and three black quarter-turn ticks on the band. The thread is right-handed (tightens clockwise seen from above) and advances 1.5 mm per turn. The filter starts about four turns onto the nipple (five at gasket contact) and three quarters of a turn (270 degrees) short of gasket contact, its gasket 1.1 mm above the land on the real thread (about 0.3 mm in the sim, as the fidelity notes) and its index stripe facing left; at gasket contact the stripe faces the robot, lined up with the witness line. Beside the head, on the robot's side of it, a 24-inch, 1/2-inch-drive ratchet (GearWrench 81364XP: 610.6 mm overall, head 36.8 mm wide and 17.5 mm thick, catalog weight 1.36 kg, polished chrome) with a 65 mm, 14-flute, 3/8-inch-drive cap-type filter wrench (Parts Unlimited 3801-0295) on its drive through a 1/2 to 3/8-inch adapter (GearWrench 81354, 35 mm long) lies on the bench cap down, 1.45 kg in all: the cap's center 13 cm from the filter's axis toward the robot (x 17.2, y 27.7), its handle running from the cap at 280 degrees (counterclockwise from +x), toward the robot's right, so its end is near x 28, y -31. Nothing else is on the bench.
scoring: The filter's angle is measured from gasket contact, positive when tightened past it (it starts at -270 degrees). The trial scores 1.0 when the filter ends 240 to 360 degrees past contact, was never past 360 degrees, no hand is on it, and the wrench has been lifted off and laid on the bench with no hand holding it, held for 1 s: the makers' three quarters to one turn, less 30 degrees for judging it by hand against the can's quarter-turn ticks. It scores 0.5 when the filter ends 180 to 240 degrees past contact, close to the makers' figure. It also scores 0.5 when it ends 240 degrees or more past contact but went past 360 degrees (never 450): past the most any maker allows, but not crushed. A result that would score 1.0 scores 0.5 while a hand is still on the filter, because a hand on it can still turn it either way. It also scores 0.5 while the wrench is still on the filter or in a hand: the job is not finished. It scores 0.25 when the filter ends 90 to 180 degrees past contact: sealing, but at most two thirds of the makers' figure, so it can still loosen. Otherwise it scores 0, including doing nothing and ending under 90 degrees past contact (a third of the least any maker asks), which can loosen under vibration. The whole trial scores 0 if the filter ever comes off its thread (4.25 turns back from its start): the fit is undone and restarting it risks cross-threading. The whole trial scores 0 if the filter is ever more than 450 degrees (1.25 turns) past contact, because the gasket is over-compressed and can roll out of its groove; backing off does not restore it. The sim does not deform the gasket, so the peak angle is the proxy. The whole trial scores 0 if more than 45 degrees of the turning past contact was done neither by a holding hand's own wrist roll nor by the wrench while a hand held it, because a swipe or knock has no control of where it stops; the 45 degrees cover the filter settling as the hand lets go. A hand holds the filter when its fingers are closed on the can, their opening stopped by its 6.6 cm width. A second hand near or on the can never voids the holding hand's turning. A hand is on the filter at the end when it holds the can or its palm or fingers touch it, with a 2 mm contact gap (the solver's resting gap); a hovering hand is not on it. Arm positions are not scored. Possible scores: 0, 0.25, 0.5, 1.0. In a real trial, before the start, spin the filter to gasket contact, draw a witness line across the can and the head, back it off three quarters of a turn, and tape a protractor ring with 15-degree marks around the land. Afterwards read the line against the ring (whole turns from the video), check the video for a swipe and a hand left on the can, then put a click torque wrench set to 18 N·m on the cap and turn it clockwise: it must click before the can moves (the specified torque was reached; if the can moves first, the trial scores at most 0.5). Inspect the gasket for a flattened or rolled lip.
reset_notes: Unscrew the filter, wipe and re-oil its gasket, spin it back on to gasket contact, check the witness lines meet, and back it off three quarters of a turn. Replace the filter if it was tightened past a full turn (its gasket is deformed). Lay the wrench back on the bench on its tape outline, cap down, handle along the outline.
fidelity: Past contact the gasket's torque rises linearly to 18 N·m at 0.75 turn (Kawasaki's figure), 29 N·m at 1.25 turns. A hand on the can slips at about 2.5 N·m, so the wrench does the rest. The cap is drawn only: centered on the can it is held on the flutes and drives it through a 400 N·m/rad spring; the ratchet freewheels back. 18 N·m is 1.7 times the arms' rated two-hand torque (10.7 N·m) and 76% of their peak (23.8), used in short strokes. No oil or gasket deformation is simulated.
scores: Dream-1 run: PENDING (2,400 steps); demo: 1.0 (1,919 steps)
